system_overview: This specification models a classic balance scale puzzle, often presented as a problem from the American radio program Car Talk. Given a stone of a specified total weight and a balance scale, the task is to cut the stone into a specified number of pieces so that one can weigh any object with an integral weight from one up to the total weight. The key insight is that pieces can be placed on both sides of the balance scale: placing a piece on the same side as the object being weighed effectively subtracts that piece's weight. The specification exhaustively searches all ordered partitions of the total weight into the given number of pieces and checks whether each partition can measure every required integer weight. The classic instance (total weight 40, four pieces) has the solution of pieces weighing 1, 3, 9, and 27 (powers of three), connected to balanced ternary number representation.
actors_and_components: The system consists of a balance scale and a set of stone pieces. The balance scale has two pans: one for the object being weighed and one for the reference pieces. Pieces can be placed on either pan or left off the scale entirely, giving three choices per piece. There are no concurrent actors; the specification performs a static exhaustive search over all valid partitions.
model_bounds: Two constants control the problem size: the total weight of the stone and the number of pieces it is cut into. For the classic problem these are 40 and 4 respectively. The specification can handle other values, though computation time grows significantly for larger inputs.
additional_assumptions: The specification operates entirely at the assumption level rather than as a state machine. It evaluates an assumption formula at startup that searches all ordered (non-decreasing) partitions of the total weight into the specified number of pieces. For each partition, it checks whether every integer weight from one to the total weight can be expressed as a linear combination of the piece weights using coefficients from the set {negative one, zero, positive one}, corresponding to placing each piece on the opposite pan, leaving it off, or placing it on the same pan as the object. If a valid partition is found, it is printed; otherwise a no-solution message is printed. The search considers only non-decreasing sequences to avoid redundant permutation checking.
